h1: Brewing classes as a taproom revenue line
title: Brewing Classes for Taproom Revenue | Craft Beer School
desc: How to cost, price and run brewing classes in a brewpub so quiet hours earn money, with the excise questions to settle first.
teaser: A Saturday morning brewhouse earns nothing. A brewing class for twelve people changes that, if you cost it honestly.
standfirst: Brewing classes fill the hours when a taproom is empty and turn regulars into people who care about your beer. They only pay if you count the brewer's time, the beer you pour and the rules on who may brew on licensed premises.
sections: A class turns quiet hours into paid seats

Most taprooms do their trade in the evening and on weekend afternoons. A Saturday morning or a weekday afternoon is dead time: the rent is still running, the brewhouse is clean and nobody is at the bar. A brewing class puts paying guests in the room during exactly those hours.

The arithmetic fits on a napkin. As an illustration, say you run a class for 12 people at ₹2,500 a head. That is ₹30,000 a session before costs. Malt, hops and yeast for a 50 litre demonstration batch cost a small fraction of that. The real costs are staff time, the tasting flight you pour and whatever food you include. Run it twice a month and you have a line on the profit and loss statement that did not exist before, earned in hours that used to earn nothing.
Pick a format your brewer can run without stopping production

Three formats work in a brewpub. They differ mainly in how much brewer time they eat.

  • Talk and taste, about 90 minutes. Grain to chew, hops to rub, a walk past the tanks and four small tasting pours. No brewing. The easiest to staff.
  • Demonstration brew, 3 to 4 hours. The brewer runs a small pilot batch while guests weigh grain, stir the mash and taste wort at each stage.
  • Hands-on brew day, 5 to 6 hours. Guests do the work in small teams on a pilot kit, from milling to pitching yeast.

A single infusion mash takes around 60 minutes and a typical boil another 60, so anything with real brewing in it needs half a day. Never run a class on the main brewhouse during a production brew. Hot wort, caustic and a crowd do not mix. A 20 to 50 litre pilot system on its own bench is the right tool.
Price the seat from the cost of the hour

Work out what one session really costs before you pick a price. List it line by line:

  • Brewer and assistant time, including set-up and cleaning afterwards. A 4 hour class is usually 6 hours of labour.
  • Ingredients for the pilot batch.
  • The tasting flight. Four 100 ml pours per guest is 400 ml each, so 4.8 litres for 12 guests.
  • Food, printed notes and any take-home item such as a branded glass.
  • Gas, water and power for the pilot kit.

Value the beer at what it would have sold for over the bar, not at your brewing cost. If those litres would have sold anyway, the class has to beat that. Then set the seat price so a session at two thirds full still covers every line. Classes rarely sell out every time, least of all in the monsoon months.
The beer guests brew is still excise beer

This is the part founders skip. Beer brewed on licensed brewpub or microbrewery premises falls under the state excise regime, whoever stirred the mash. Every litre has to sit inside your production records. Taking it home is governed by the same takeaway rules as any other sale, which many states restrict. Some states also care about who may enter a licensed brewing area at all.

Rules vary by state and change, so check the current notification for your state or ask a licensing consultant before you advertise anything. The safe design is a class where guests brew a batch that becomes part of your taproom stock. They come back in two to three weeks to drink it on site. That return visit is a second spend you would not otherwise get.
Sell it to the people already at your bar

Your regulars are the first market. A table card and a word from staff at the bar sell more seats than a paid advert. Corporate teams are the second: one office booking for 15 people fills a weekday afternoon and usually brings a food order with it. Our guide to paid brewery tours covers the same audience from a lighter angle.

Gift vouchers sell well before Diwali and in December. Keep the group to 10 to 15 people. Above 20, the guests at the back of a pilot kit see nothing and the brewer turns into a lecturer. Keep tasting pours small and spread them through the session. Put water and soft drinks on the table from the start and make sure nobody who has been tasting drives home.
Track the class like a beer, not a favour

Give classes their own line in the accounts so you can see whether they pay. Record seats sold, ticket revenue, labour hours, litres poured and what class guests spend at the bar afterwards. A class that only breaks even on tickets but sends 12 people to the bar for dinner is doing its job. One that ties up your brewer on a day the tanks needed attention is not.

That is the gap between a fun idea and a revenue line: costing labour honestly, pricing for a part-full room and folding the result into a model of taproom economics that already carries your rent and wages. Start this week by costing one 90 minute talk and taste session line by line, then offer it to ten regulars before you print a single flyer.
faqs: Can guests take home the beer they brew in a class?
It depends on your state's excise rules for takeaway sales from a brewpub, which many states restrict. The safer design is to serve the batch in your taproom and invite the class back to drink it.
How many people should a brewing class take?
Ten to fifteen works well on a 20 to 50 litre pilot kit. Above about twenty, people at the back cannot see or take part.
Do I need a separate pilot system to run classes?
It is strongly advisable. Running a class on the production brewhouse mixes guests with hot wort and caustic and puts a production batch at risk.
